title: Command Pattern
oneLiner: Turns a request into a standalone object, so it can be queued, logged, retried, or undone instead of executed immediately.

hero.name: Invoker
hero.catchphrase: Don't just do it — wrap it, queue it, undo it.
hero.power: Wraps an action and its arguments into an object, so the action can be delayed, queued, logged, or reversed.
hero.weakness: Wrapping a single, immediate, one-off action in a full command object is pure ceremony — sometimes a direct method call is exactly right.
hero.origin: Invoker was summoned when a design tool's 'undo' button had nothing to undo — every action had already executed and vanished the instant the user clicked.

story.problem: A drawing app calls `canvas.drawShape(shape)` directly from the button handler. Once drawn, there's no record of what happened — 'undo' has nothing to work with.
story.solution: Invoker wraps each action in a `DrawCommand` object with both `execute()` and `undo()`. The app pushes every executed command onto a history stack.
story.result: Undo just pops the last command and calls `.undo()`. Redo, macros, and action logging all become trivial once actions are objects instead of side effects.

before: Actions execute immediately with no record
No way to undo, redo, or replay anything
Button handlers are tightly coupled to canvas internals
after: Every action is an object with execute() and undo()
Undo/redo is just popping a history stack
Button handlers only know about commands, not canvas internals

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A user clicks Undo. Nothing happens — the app has no idea what the last action even was.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Every button just calls canvas.drawShape() directly. There's no record of anything. How do we even build Undo?

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: Invoker appears holding a small, labeled box — an action, wrapped and ready to replay.
panels.speaker: Invoker
panels.dialogue: Stop executing actions and forgetting them. Wrap every action in an object. Then I can queue it, log it, or reverse it.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: DrawCommand holds execute() and undo(). Every executed command is pushed onto a history stack.
panels.speaker: Invoker
panels.dialogue: Execute a command, push it to history. Undo just pops the last one and calls its own undo(). It already knows how to reverse itself.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: Undo, redo, and an action log all work correctly, built entirely on the same command objects.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Undo, redo, even a full action replay log — all came nearly for free once actions became objects.

useWhen: You need undo/redo, and actions must be reversible objects rather than fire-and-forget calls.
You want to queue, schedule, or log requests instead of executing them immediately.
You're building macros or batch operations composed of many smaller actions.
avoidWhen: The action is simple, immediate, and never needs to be undone, queued, or logged — a direct call is simpler.
You'd need to wrap dozens of trivial one-off actions just to satisfy the pattern, with no real payoff.
The overhead of designing a clean `undo()` for every command outweighs the benefit for your use case.
commonMistakes: Implementing `execute()` without a matching, correct `undo()` — half an undo system is worse than none, since it misleads users.
Letting commands hold onto stale references (a deleted shape, a closed connection), causing `undo()` to fail silently.
Wrapping trivial actions in commands 'for consistency' when a plain function call was clearly sufficient.
Letting the command history grow unbounded in memory without ever trimming it.
explanation.realWorldExample: Undo/redo stacks in editors (text, image, code), task queues where jobs are serialized command objects, and GUI menu items/buttons that wrap the same underlying action (so a Ctrl+Z and a menu click trigger identical behavior) are all Command.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Isn't this just calling a function later instead of now?

conversation.speaker: Invoker
conversation.message: It's more than delay — it's that the ACTION ITSELF becomes an object with state. I can inspect it, log it, queue it behind other commands, or ask it to reverse itself. A bare function call can't do any of that.

conversation.speaker: Invoker
conversation.message: When the action is a one-shot, unreversible, immediate thing — like reading a value. Wrapping that in a command object is just extra ceremony.

codeBattle.scenario: Your job-processing system needs to accept tasks from users, queue them, retry failed ones, and log exactly what was requested and when.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: Invoker turns each job request into a queueable, retryable, loggable object instead of an immediate function call that vanishes once executed.

quiz.question: What does the Command pattern turn a request into?
options: A standalone object with its own execute (and often undo) behavior
A single global function that can never be reused
A subclass of the object it acts on
quiz.answer: A standalone object with its own execute (and often undo) behavior
quiz.explanation: Making the request itself an object is exactly what enables queuing, logging, and undo.

quiz.question: How does Command typically enable undo functionality?
options: Each command implements its own undo() logic, and a history stack tracks executed commands to reverse
It automatically reverses any change made to any variable in the program
It relies on the operating system's built-in undo feature
Undo is unrelated to the Command pattern
quiz.answer: Each command implements its own undo() logic, and a history stack tracks executed commands to reverse
quiz.explanation: The command knows how to reverse itself; the history stack just decides which one to reverse next.

quiz.question: When is Command overkill?
options: When the action is simple, immediate, and will never need to be queued, logged, or undone
When you're building an undo/redo system
When you need to queue tasks for later execution
When you're logging every user action for auditing
quiz.answer: When the action is simple, immediate, and will never need to be queued, logged, or undone
quiz.explanation: Wrapping a trivial, one-off action in a command object adds ceremony without a matching benefit.

quiz.question: What's a common mistake when implementing Command?
options: Implementing execute() without a correct, matching undo(), producing a broken or misleading undo system
Giving every command an execute() method
Storing executed commands in a history stack
Using commands for queued background jobs
quiz.answer: Implementing execute() without a correct, matching undo(), producing a broken or misleading undo system
quiz.explanation: A command that can't reliably reverse itself defeats the purpose of offering undo at all.
